title: Celsus describes the prophets of Phoenicia and Palestine
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν τρόπον τῶν ἐν Φοινίκῃ καὶ Παλαιστίνῃ μαντείων ἐπαγγέλλεται φράσειν ὁ Κέλσος ὡς ἀκούσας καὶ πάνυ καταμαθὼν, φέρε καὶ ταῦτα κατανοήσωμεν. πρῶτον δὴ λέγει πλείονα εἶναι εἴδη προφητειῶν, μὴ ἐκτιθέμενος αὐτά· οὐδὲ γὰρ εἶχεν, ἀλλὰ ψευδῶς ἐπανετείνετο. ὃ δέ φησιν εἶναι τελεώτατον παρὰ τοῖς τῇδε ἀνδράσιν ἴδωμεν. πολλοὶ, φησὶ. καὶ ἀνώνυμοι ῥᾷστα ἐκ τῆς προστυχούσης αἰτίας καὶ ἐν ἱεροῖς καὶ ἔξω ἱερῶν. οἱ δὲ καὶ ἀγείραντες καὶ ἐπιφοιτῶντες πόλεσιν ἢ στρατοπέδοις, κινοῦνται δῆθεν ὡς θεσπίζοντες. πρόχειρον δ᾿ ἑκάστῳ καὶ σύνηθες εἰπεῖν· ἐγὼ ὁ θεός εἰμι ἢ θεοῦ παῖς ἢ πνεῦμα θεῖον. ἥκω δέ· ἤδη γὰρ ὁ κόσμος ἀπόλλυται, καὶ ὑμεῖς, ὦ ἄνθρωποι, διὰ τὰς ἀδικίας οἴχεσθε. ἐγὼ δὲ σῶσαι θέλω· καὶ ὄψεσθέ με αὖθις μετ᾿ οὐρανίου δυνάμεως ἐπανιόντα. μακάριος ὁ νῦν με θρησκεύσας, τοῖς δ᾿ ἄλλοις ἅπασι πῦρ αἰώνιον ἐπιβαλῶ καὶ πόλεσι καὶ χώραις. καὶ ἄνθρωποι, οἳ μὴ τὰς ἑαυτῶν ποινὰς ἴσασι, μεταγνώσονται μάτην καὶ στενάξουσι· τοὺς δέ μοι πεισθέντας αἰωνίους φυλάξω. εἶτα τούτοις ἑξῆς φησι· ταῦτ᾿ ἐπανατεινάμενοι προστιθέασιν ἐφεξῆς ἄγνωστα καὶ πάροιστρα καὶ πάντῃ ἄδηλα, ὧν τὸ μὲν γνῶμα οὐδεὶς ἂν ἔχων νοῦν εὑρεῖν δύναιτο· ἀσαφῆ γὰρ καὶ τὸ μηδὲν, ἀνοήτῳ δὲ ἢ γόητι παντὶ περὶ παντὸς ἀφορμὴν ἐνδίδωσιν, ὅπῃ βούλεται, τὸ λεχθὲν σφετερίζεσθαι.
pass_a_gloss: Since Celsus also announces that he will tell (φράζω) the manner (τρόπος) of the oracles (μαντεῖον) in Phoenicia and Palestine, as having heard and thoroughly learned (καταμανθάνω), come, let us consider (κατανοέω) these too. First he says there are more kinds (εἶδος) of prophecies, not setting them out (ἐκτίθημι); for he did not have [them], but falsely (ψευδῶς) held it out. And what he says is most perfect among the men there, let us see. [Celsus:] 'Many,' he says, 'and nameless (ἀνώνυμος), most easily (ῥᾷστα), from the chance (προστυγχάνω) cause (αἰτία), both in temples (ἱερόν) and outside temples; and others both begging (ἀγείρω) and frequenting (ἐπιφοιτάω) cities or camps (στρατόπεδον), are moved (κινέω), forsooth (δῆθεν), as prophesying (θεσπίζω). Ready (πρόχειρος) to each and customary (σύνηθης) to say: I am the God, or a child (παῖς) of God, or a divine spirit. And I have come; for already the world (κόσμος) is perishing (ἀπόλλυμαι), and you, O men, because of your injustices (ἀδικία) are gone (οἴχομαι). And I wish to save (σῴζω); and you will see me again returning (ἐπάνειμι) with heavenly (οὐράνιος) power (δύναμις). Blessed (μακάριος) the one who now worshipped (θρησκεύω) me; on all the others I will cast eternal fire (πῦρ αἰώνιον), both on cities and on lands (χώρα). And men, who do not know their own penalties (ποινή), will repent (μεταγιγνώσκω) in vain and groan (στενάζω); but those persuaded by me I will guard (φυλάσσω) eternal.' Then next to these he says: 'Having held out these, they add next unknown (ἄγνωστος), frenzied (πάροιστρος) and wholly unclear (ἄδηλος) things, of which the sense (γνῶμα) no one having mind (νοῦς) could find; for [they are] obscure (ἀσαφής) and nothing (τὸ μηδέν), but to every senseless man (ἀνόητος) or sorcerer (γόης) they give a starting point (ἀφορμή) about anything, in whatever way he wishes, to appropriate (σφετερίζομαι) what was said.'
pass_b_english: Since Celsus also promises to describe the manner of the oracles in Phoenicia and Palestine, as one who has heard them and learned all about them, come, let us look at this too. First he says that there are several kinds of prophecy, but he does not set them out; for he had none to set out, and was only making a false show. But let us see what he says is the most perfect kind among the men of that region.

“Many nameless men,” he says, “very readily and on any chance occasion, both in temples and outside temples, and others who go begging and roam about cities or army camps, are stirred, so they make out, as though uttering oracles. Each has ready on his lips the customary words: ‘I am God, or a son of God, or a divine spirit. And I have come; for already the world is perishing, and you, O men, are going to ruin because of your wrongdoing. But I wish to save you. And you will see me coming back again with heavenly power. Blessed is he who worships me now; but on all the rest I will cast eternal fire, on cities and on lands alike. And men who do not know the punishments in store for them will repent in vain and groan; but those who have been persuaded by me I will keep for ever.’”

Then next he says: “Having brandished all this, they go on to add unintelligible, frenzied and altogether obscure words, whose meaning no one with any sense could discover; for they are unclear and mean nothing, but they give any fool or sorcerer an opening to seize on what was said and make it his own, on any matter and in whatever way he wishes.”

choices.choice: Everything from ‘There are many nameless men’ to the end of the chapter, except Origen’s ‘he says’ and ‘Then next he says’, is Celsus’s own wording and is in double quotation marks; the speech he puts in the mouths of these prophets is set in single quotation marks inside his. The opening report that there are ‘several kinds of prophecy’ and that one is ‘most perfect’ is indirect and left unquoted. ἐγὼ ὁ θεός εἰμι is the speaker’s claim to be the supreme God, so ‘God’ is capitalised; ‘a son of God’ and ‘a divine spirit’ are left lower-case because they are the generic claims Celsus mocks. The copy-text punctuation πολλοί, φησί. καὶ ἀνώνυμοι is read as one continuous clause. The sentence is loose Greek: πολλοὶ ... καὶ ἀνώνυμοι ... οἱ δὲ καὶ ἀγείραντες ... κινοῦνται; the English keeps both groups as subjects of ‘are stirred’. δῆθεν rendered ‘so they make out’. Several phrases in the prophets’ speech (returning ‘with heavenly power’, ‘eternal fire’, ‘blessed is he’) resemble Gospel language (compare Matthew 24:30; 25:41); they are Celsus’s caricature, not quotations by Origen, so they are not cited inline (possible allusions only). ἐπανατεινάμενοι (‘holding up, holding out’, often as a threat) rendered ‘having brandished all this’, since what is held out includes promises as well as threats. ἄγνωστα rendered ‘unintelligible’. περὶ παντός is taken with ἀφορμήν (‘an opening on any matter’).
ψευδῶς ἐπανετείνετο: 'was only making a false show' (οὐδὲ γὰρ εἶχεν: 'he had none to set out')
Celsus's opening sentence regrammared ('Many nameless men ... and others who go begging ... are stirred'); the earlier 'There are many men who ... and some who ... are stirred' did not parse
τὰς ἑαυτῶν ποινάς: 'the punishments in store for them'
ταῦτ᾿ ἐπανατεινάμενοι: 'having brandished all this' (the speech holds promises too, so not 'threats' only)
ἄγνωστα: 'unintelligible' instead of the inverted 'words unknown'
last clause recast so περὶ παντός goes with the opening, not with 'what was said': 'an opening to seize on what was said and make it his own, on any matter and in whatever way he wishes'
Celsus's words and the inner prophet speech checked for quotation marks and attributions
